entries.note: “Basically just like humans” specifies neither the relevant dimensions nor the required degree of similarity.

entries.test: Public implementation details and controlled experiments could establish whether systems with explicit models of presidential tenure avoid overlapping-tenure errors and whether LLM outputs depend entirely on statistical generation without factual constraints.
entries.note: The conditional describes a general mechanism and capability, rather than an uncertain future possibility. The universal wording makes counterexamples relevant.

entries.test: Public reproducible experiments and mechanistic analyses could establish whether the British prime minister errors result from word-pattern generation without a usable representation of the relevant historical facts.
entries.note: Reproducing the errors alone would not establish the asserted cause.
“Hasn’t put the time in” supplies no shared threshold for sufficient research effort or computational progress.

entries.test: Public architecture documentation and repeated factual reliability evaluations could establish whether systems lacking world models persistently produce confidently stated falsehoods.
entries.note: In context, “authoritative bullshit” refers to confident factual errors. “Never stops” asserts their persistence, rather than an error in every response.

entries.test: Public evaluations or documented deployments could show whether outsourcing multistep jobs to LLM agents produces consequential task failures attributable to deficiencies in their world models.
entries.note: The plain forecast is that these deficiencies will have practical consequences for delegated multistep work. No deadline is given.

entries.test: Public task evaluations and prospective validation studies could show both successful and unsuccessful substitution for human performance and whether any reliable method identifies which will occur before execution.
entries.note: “Never know in advance” is an absolute claim about predictability, not merely a warning that failures sometimes occur.
